item.title: Carry out your long march, but offer an alternative for gas, power
item.description:
Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) Acting Secretary General and Political Adviser to the Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Ruhul Kabir Rizvi has called upon the Opposition not to threaten street protests over the gas and electricity crisis, but to present alternative plans and recommendations in Parliament on how the shortages can be addressed.

He said the country’s gas and electricity crisis had been caused by the US-Iran war and the previous government’s flawed planning.

Rizvi made the remarks as the chief guest at the induction ceremony of the newly elected executive committee of the Bangladesh Dance Artistes Association, held at the Jatiya Natyashala Auditorium (national theatre hall) of Shilpakala Academy in Dhaka on Friday afternoon.

“You can hold a long march or announce programmes over gas and electricity—that is fine. But tell us an alternative: how are we going to supply gas and electricity? Where will we get them from, and how will we get them?” Rizvi said.

He further said the Opposition should present a plan outlining what steps should be taken to tackle the current crisis. According to him, Opposition MPs have the opportunity to speak in Parliament.

While criticising the government and holding programmes outside Parliament are normal practices in a democracy, he said, the Opposition should also offer constructive recommendations for addressing the crisis.

The Prime Minister’s political adviser further said, “I do not think it would be right to deliberately create a planned paralysis. Rather, a plan must be put forward on how this crisis can be brought to an end.”

He also warned that if the activities of the past were repeated, the country would be pushed further into darkness.

Pointing to global conflicts and disruptions to the energy supply chain as factors behind the current gas and electricity crisis, Ruhul Kabir Rizvi said difficulties had arisen in importing the fuel needed because the transportation of energy through the Strait of Hormuz had been disrupted.

NCP steps up street protests alongside parliament, long marches and mass rally ahead

He claimed that the crisis had not been caused by any action of the government itself.

Rizvi also highlighted the role of songs and dance during the July uprising. He said cultural performances had inspired and emboldened protesters during the movement.

The event was chaired by Bangladesh Dance Artistes Association President Farhana Baby.

State Minister for Road Transport and Railways Habib Ur Rashid Habib, BNP Cultural Affairs Secretary Ashraf Uddin Ujjal, poet Rezauddin Stalin, actor Helal Khan and Zakir Hossain Rukon, among others, attended as special guests.

The newly elected executive committee members of the Bangladesh Dance Artistes Association were later formally inducted.

‘Country will fall behind without equal participation of boys and girls’

Speaking at another programme, BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi said the country and society will fall behind unless boys and girls were ensured equal participation in every field, including sports.

He made the remarks as the chief guest at the inaugural ceremony of an inter-divisional Under-16 girls’ football competition organised by the Bangladesh Women’s Sports Association this morning.

Rizvi said, “We know that there are many barriers in our society. But if we are to keep pace with the progress of the world, our girls must come forward, particularly in the field of sports. If we can produce a great athlete among our girls, it will hold our heads high in the eyes of the world. It will also inspire women in other sectors.”

Jamaat warns govt of public backlash if Opposition long march is obstructed

The BNP acting secretary general further said men and women must move forward on an equal footing in every field. Otherwise, he said, the country would fall behind.

“Our Prime Minister has strongly recognised this issue. That is why he has introduced the Notun Kuri Sports programme. Those who are deserving must be given due recognition. Competitions of this kind should be organised in every metropolitan area and district,” he stated.

The Prime Minister’s political adviser also said efforts were under way to establish a sports university in Bangladesh.

In her welcome address, Bangladesh Women’s Sports Association President Sarwat Siraj said there was no alternative to women’s participation in sports if Bangladesh’s nationalist forces were to move forward against “extreme conservatism, religious fanaticism and forces selling tickets to heaven”.

She said the Bangladesh Women’s Sports Association was working towards this goal.

item.title: Prairies, parks, and padfoots: My summer with Canada Geese
item.description:
Coming this far into the Prairies to attend a scientific conference was quite an undertaking, but getting to admire the beauty of Canada Geese each morning near my hotel was deeply rewarding. I could not have asked for anything more precious.
During a two-week stay at a downtown Saskatoon hotel in the summer of 2019, it became a daily routine to encounter gaggles of geese foraging along the South Saskatchewan River. The more I watched them, the more captivated I became by their distinct features. These birds are abundant throughout Saskatoon, particularly along the Meewasin Valley Trail.
Canada Geese grazing near South Saskatchewan River in Saskatoon. Native to North America, these large waterfowl are easily recognized by their long black necks, black heads, and striking white `chinstrap` facial patches. Highly adaptable, they frequently forage on manicured lawns in urban parks. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Throughout the day, I frequently crossed paths with flocks on the grassy waterfront stretches of Kiwanis Park, the manicured lawns of Spadina Crescent East, and in the river itself. As I walked beneath the mature ash and elm canopy along the paved trails flanking the west bank, seeing these geese became a constant and comforting sight.
For about two weeks, I stayed at Delta Hotels Saskatoon Downtown on Twentieth Street East, nestled in Saskatoon’s central business district near the scenic river pathways. The 18-storey structure, originally built in 1983 as the Ramada Renaissance Hotel, is one of the tallest buildings in Saskatoon. It was later renamed the Radisson Hotel Saskatoon before undergoing its most recent transformation. In January 2019, just six months before my visit, the property was rebranded under Marriott International’s Delta Hotels banner.
Two Canada Geese standing on a grassy stretch next to a gravel path along the waterfront at Kiwanis Memorial Park. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
As a guest in Room 619, I frequently encountered Canada Geese in the immediate vicinity of the hotel. Staying just 650 metres from Kiwanis Memorial Park and the sprawling waterfront lawns along the South Saskatchewan River, I was virtually guaranteed to cross paths with them every day.
Located practically across the street and stretching within a few short blocks of the hotel, the beautifully manicured green space of Kiwanis Park on the river’s west bank serves as a primary foraging ground, where gaggles of geese graze on open lawns throughout the day.
The iconic urban canopy of American elm trees shading the brick-paved promenade along Spadina Crescent East. This vibrant Saskatoon riverfront stretch runs right next to Kiwanis Memorial Park, sloping down toward the South Saskatchewan River on the left and the downtown street on the right. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Furthermore, the paved Meewasin Valley Trail runs directly along the riverbank, just steps from the hotel lobby. Along nearby Spadina Crescent East, the geese routinely moved between the river and urban park lawns, occasionally halting downtown traffic as they crossed the busy street.
While Canada Geese have earned a notorious reputation for being cantankerous, fiercely territorial, and hostile towards humans, I pleasantly discovered that this downtown Saskatoon flock was highly urbanized and remarkably calm. They comfortably foraged beside the paved walking paths, paying little attention to me as I photographed them.
A flock of six geese grazing on the riverside lawns of Kiwanis Memorial Park, right besides a winding, paved pedestrian pathway. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
One afternoon, I spotted a few goslings along a stretch of the South Saskatchewan River shoreline, though I missed the opportunity to take a photo. Because it was already late July, I had also missed the chance to witness the local “crèches” by about a month. Had my visit taken place between May and June, I would have had a much better chance of seeing these massive gosling broods along the Meewasin Trail.
During those spring months, dominant adult pairs frequently form cooperative daycares, herding groups of up to 60 fuzzy goslings along pathways and across local streets.
A pair of Canada Geese by the water`s edge, surrounded by tall, dry grasses and reeds. One stands alert while the other rests on the bank, casting a sharp reflection in the calm water. This quiet marshland represents their traditional nesting and foraging habitat. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Had I been in the Canadian Prairies a couple of months earlier, I probably would have witnessed many more goslings than I actually did. Goslings typically hatch in May, resulting in crowded and highly active family scenes along the riverbanks. By mid-summer, geese undergo their annual moult and temporarily lose their flight feathers, meaning they spend considerable time walking around public parks and paths rather than flying.
One afternoon, while sitting on a park bench, I watched a flock of geese frolicking and noticed the distinct physical features that set them apart from other birds. They have solid black heads and long, elegant black necks. Their signature bright white “chinstrap” is impossible to miss — a stark patch running across the throat and up the sides of the face. Their breasts range from light brown to grayish, contrasting beautifully with the scalloped, tan-edged feathers along their backs and wings. Completing their striking appearance, their large webbed feet are deep dark grey or black.
Goslings swimming between two adult Canada Geese. Such large group is known as a crèche. Canada geese frequently combine their goslings into a single “nursery” guarded by a few adult `babysitters`. Cooperative parenting behavior distributes the heavy duty of predator surveillance across fewer adults, dramatically increasing the survival rate of the young goslings. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
That summer 2019 visit to the Canadian Prairies also took me to Alberta. On a road trip from Saskatoon to Edmonton, it drizzled almost the entire way. As I travelled along the Yellowhead Highway (Highway 16), which cuts through the agricultural aspen parkland and prairie regions, I spotted gaggles of geese around many canola fields and prairie sloughs — shallow, swampy wetlands.
Once I reached Edmonton, however, my busy schedule with other commitments did not allow me to visit some of the urban green spaces where I could probably have seen larger goose broods.
Five Canada Geese lined up along the grassy banks of the South Saskatchewan River. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Both Saskatchewan and Alberta lie within the “Prairie Pothole Region” and the “Mississippi-Central Flyways”, making them home to some of the highest concentrations of Canada Geese in North America. The regions serve as major migratory hubs as well as permanent breeding grounds.
After reading some literature on geese, I learned that the Canada Goose is widely considered one of the ultimate wildlife conservation success stories, having recovered from near extinction in the early 20th century to a thriving population of millions across North America today.
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, unchecked hunting, habitat loss, and the widespread use of geese as live hunting decoys decimated their populations. Backed by protective measures such as the Migratory Birds Convention Act, aggressive captive-breeding programs and the release of former live decoys helped restore the species across the continent.
Humans also altered the North American landscape in ways that have favoured the survival traits of the Canada Goose. Freshly mowed suburban lawns, corporate parks, golf courses, and agricultural fields now provide prime, nutrient-rich grazing grounds. Human development has also eliminated many major natural predators, removing one of the primary threats to adult geese.
Consequently, many urban goose populations have lost their migratory instincts entirely. Because urban retention ponds and parks rarely freeze completely, millions of geese remain year-round residents of cities.

Home minister: All citizens to enjoy equal rights based on citizenship
item.description:
Home Affairs Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has said no community in Bangladesh needs to be identified as a “minority”, as all citizens will enjoy equal rights, security and freedom based on citizenship rather than religion or any other identity.
“Our primary and foremost identity should be that we are all Bangladeshis,” he said.
The minister made the remarks while addressing the inaugural ceremony of the Historic Central Janmashtami Procession at the Dhakeshwari National Temple premises here today, marking the Central Janmashtami Festival 1433.
Calling for a non-communal Bangladesh, Salahuddin said the government’s fundamental policy is “Bangladesh for everyone” and that religious, social and ethnic identities should come afterwards.
He said religious freedom and observance for people of all faiths had been ensured since the present government assumed office six months ago.
Referring to the Constitution, the minister said the state is obligated to ensure religious freedom for every citizen and that no discrimination can be made on the basis of religion.
He also urged people to replace the term “communal harmony” with “religious and social harmony, coexistence and peace”.
Mahanagar Sarbajanin Puja Committee President Gopal Chandra Debnath presided over the programme, while Dhaka South City Corporation Administrator Bir Muktijoddha Md Abdus Salam attended the procession by lighting a ceremonial lamp.
Bijon Kanti Sarker, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister (status of State Minister), on Hindu, Buddhist, Christian and Ethnic Affairs and lawmaker from Dhaka-07 constituency Hamidur Rahman were present there as guests of honour.
The procession began from plassey intersection and concluded at Bahadur Shah Park in the old Dhaka.

item.title: AC Land’s raid on journalist’s home under probe in Kurigram
item.description:
A three-member committee has been formed to investigate Rowmari Assistant Commissioner (Land) Rafiur Rahman’s raid on the home of a local journalist in Kurigram, amid allegations that he targeted the journalist in retaliation for questioning one of his decisions.
The raid was reportedly conducted to search for drugs, but no drugs were found during the operation on Thursday.
The Kurigram district administration formed the committee following a call from the ministry seeking information about the incident. It will determine whether Rafiur had any ulterior motive in carrying out the operation at the home of Rafiqul Islam Saju, Rowmari upazila correspondent of the daily Manab Zamin.
The committee, headed by Kurigram Additional District Magistrate (Revenue) and with Rowmari Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Mahbubul Hasan as its member secretary, has been asked to submit its report by Sunday, Kurigram Deputy Commissioner Annapurna Deb Nath said.
The raid took place around 11am on Thursday when Rafiur went to Saju’s home in Sabuj Para accompanied by two police officers and several Ansar members.
Rafiur said he conducted the operation based on specific information. However, no drugs were found during the search, and he left without making any recovery.
Saju and local journalists alleged that household belongings were searched and left scattered during the operation.
Saju alleged that Rafiur conducted the raid without prior approval and with the intention of harassing him.
He said the AC Land became angry after Saju questioned him by phone on Wednesday about the cancellation of a citizen’s land mutation just three days after it had been completed, without issuing a notice or holding a hearing.
“He deliberately conducted the raid at my home to frame me out of a desire for revenge. It was illegal,” Saju alleged.
UNO Mahbubul Hasan said Rafiur had been assigned to oversee a fertilizer distribution point but went to Saju’s home on the way.
“He did not inform me before conducting the raid. I learned about it after the operation,” the UNO said.
Deputy Commissioner Annapurna Deb Nath said the ministry contacted her after reports about the raid were published.
Asked about allegations of retaliation, she said the investigation would determine whether Rafiur had an ulterior motive.
“There may have been some mischief involved. We had received some complaints against him earlier. He has already been transferred for this reason,” she said.
Rafiur has already been transferred and attached to the office of the Dhaka divisional commissioner following allegations of irregularities, including alleged bribery in land services and abuse of power.
Local journalists alleged that Rafiur had been angered by reports about his alleged irregularities and had targeted Saju and several other journalists.
The allegations have not been independently verified.

item.title: One killed, over 50 injured in Brahmanbaria clash
item.description:
A man was killed and more than 50 others were injured in a clash between two groups over a pond land dispute in Nasirnagar upazila of Brahmanbaria on Friday.
The deceased was identified as Naji Molla, son of Abdul Awal Mia.
The clash broke out on the Nasirnagar-Sarail-Lakhai regional highway near a market in Burishwar union in the afternoon, leaving the area tense.
According to police and local residents, Abdul Awal Mia and Fazu Mia’s groups in Burishwar village had a long-standing dispute over pond land for a long time. The dispute escalated into a clash between their supporters on Friday afternoon.
At one point, Naji Molla of Abdul Awal Mia’s group was struck by a spear and died at the scene.
The injured were taken to Nasirnagar Upazila Health Complex for treatment. Four people, including Abdul Awal Mia, were in critical condition and referred to Dhaka for advanced treatment. The others are Rahich Mia, Taus Mia and Kalon Mia.
After news of Naji’s death spread, members of Fazu Mia’s group fled their homes, making it impossible to immediately determine the names of those injured or involved in the clash from their side.
Tension remained high in the area following the incident. A large number of police personnel were deployed to prevent further violence and maintain law and order.
Brahmanbaria ASP Obaidur Rahman said a large number of police personnel had been deployed in the area to prevent any further clashes.

item.title: Sylhet journos boycott State Minister Humaiun Kobir over alleged harassment
item.description:
Local television journalists in Sylhet on Friday decided to boycott news coverage of State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir and the local BNP, after several media workers were harassed by political activists at the Hazrat Shahjalal Shrine.
Kobir, visiting Sylhet for the first time since taking office as state minister, offered prayers at the shrine after Jummah prayers. According to a pre-scheduled program, he was supposed to brief the media at the shrine's premises.
To facilitate the departure of devotees, mainstream media workers positioned themselves near the main gate. However, due to intense crowding and pushing by political activists, the journalists were forced to move outside the shrine area. At that point, a group of youths chanting "Ziar Sainik Ek Ho" attacked and harassed them.
Nabil Hossain, a journalist for Jamuna Television, condemned the incident on Facebook, noting that the harassers aggressively questioned how the media dared to leave without taking the minister's statement. He added that multiple media workers faced isolated harassment at the scene.
Star News Sylhet Bureau Chief Yahya Maruf said the journalists moved outside due to the chaotic crowd. "Some BNP activists then set upon us and misbehaved with the television journalists," Maruf said.
Following the incident, local television journalists unanimously decided to abstain from covering any future programs of both State Minister Kabir and the local BNP.
Meanwhile, Sylhet WASA Chairman and BNP central Assistant Organizing Secretary Miftah Siddiqui, along with Sylhet City BNP General Secretary Imdad Hossain Chowdhury, could not be reached for comment as they did not answer their phones.

item.title: Dengue: 512 dengue patients hospitalized in 24 hours last
item.description:
A total of 512 dengue patients were admitted to hospitals across the country in the last 24 hours after being infected with dengue , according to a regular report of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Of them, 280 were in Dhaka Division, 57 in Mymensingh Division, 109 in Chittagong Division, 72 in Khulna Division, 21 in Barisal Division, and 13 in Rangpur Division.
A total of 40,044 dengue patients have been hospitalized across the country this year. No one died of dengue in the last 24 hours. So far this year, 111 people have died from dengue.
In the last 24 hours, 726 patients recovered and were discharged from hospitals. So far this year, a total of 37,193 dengue patients have recovered after receiving treatment in hospitals and have been discharged.
A total of 102,861 people were infected with dengue, and 413 people died from the disease last year.

item.title: State Minister Abdul Bari sent to Dhaka for advanced treatment
item.description:
State Minister for Public Administration and Food Abdul Bari, who was injured in a road accident in Shibganj, Bogra, while travelling from Dhaka to his constituency in Joypurhat-2 (Kalai-Khetlal-Akkelpur), has been sent to Dhaka for advanced treatment.
The state minister and his wife Najma Ara Begum were injured in the accident on Friday morning. A woman, identified as Firoza Begum, 55, was killed.
Kalai Police Station Officer-in-Charge Saidul Alam said Abdul Bari received primary treatment in Kalai before being admitted to Joypurhat 400-Bed General Hospital. His wife was unharmed and is in good health.
After receiving treatment at the hospital, doctors decided to refer the state minister to Dhaka for advanced medical care. His planned visit to the constituency was cancelled, and he was taken to Dhaka by ambulance at around 12:45pm on Friday.
Dr Rashed Mobarak Jewel, superintendent of Joypurhat 400-Bed General Hospital, said Abdul Bari sustained injuries to both shoulders and his chest in the accident but is now out of danger.

item.title: Asaduzzaman urges Hindu community to unite against injustice, evil forces
item.description:
Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman on Friday urged members of the Hindu community to remain united against any evil or destructive forces and injustice, saying the government is committed to ensuring an environment where every citizen can celebrate religious festivals freely, safely and with dignity.
He made the remarks while speaking as the chief guest at a program, marking Janmashtami on the Ramgopal Temple premises in the Shailkupa upazila headquarters.
The minister called upon the Hindu community to stand beside the government against any form of evil or destructive forces. Referring to the teachings of Lord Krishna, he said Krishna appeared nearly 5,000 years ago to defeat evils and oppression and establish peace and justice in society.
“Fighting against injustice and evil forces is the core principle of his teachings. We believe that when we fight to eliminate injustice and evils from society, you will stand beside the government as you have always done,” he said.
Asaduzzaman warned that no attempt to create disorder or obstruct religious programmes will be tolerated. “Religion is for individuals, but security is for everyone. We must move forward with this eternal principle,” he said, adding that law enforcement agencies will take strict legal action against anyone attempting to create disorder, intimidation or obstruction during religious programs.
“There is no distinction between minorities and majorities. Everyone in the country must be able to practise their religions peacefully and without hindrance,” the minister said.
After the discussion, Asaduzzaman joined a colourful Janmashtami procession that began at the Ramgopal Temple and paraded through the main streets of Shailkupa town.
Jhenaidah Deputy Commissioner Md Noman Hossain, Zila Parishad Administrator Md Abdul Majid, leaders of the Puja Udjapan Parishad and Hindu devotees from different walks of life attended the program.

item.title: Commuters suffer due to transport shortage in Ctg
item.description:
The port city is facing a shortage of public transport as commuters struggle daily with inadequate buses, unfit vehicles, irregular services, traffic congestion, and rising fares.
The number of buses and minibuses operating in the city remains far below demand. Many vehicles are old and reportedly lack valid fitness certificates or route permits. The absence of designated bus stops in many areas further worsens traffic congestion.
Although the Bangladesh Road Transport Corporation (BRTC) has 72 buses in Chittagong, most operate on long-distance routes rather than serving ordinary city commuters.
A significant number of buses are also hired on a reserved basis to transport industrial workers. Consequently, commuters face long queues at major bus stops during morning office hours and in the afternoon. Even after waiting for long periods, passengers often struggle to board overcrowded buses.
According to the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA), 17 routes have been designated for bus and minibus services in the city. Around 2,900 route permits have been issued, while 803 buses are listed as lacking valid fitness certificates. Transport stakeholders, however, believe the actual number of unfit vehicles could be higher.
Yusuf Talukder, a resident of Muradpur, said office-goers suffer the most. “We have to wait for a long time for public transport in the morning and after office hours. Getting a seat often feels like a matter of luck,” he said.
Abdur Rahman of Bahaddarhat said that fares are often increased during rain or when passenger demand rises. Many buses, he said, operate on only part of their designated routes, forcing passengers to pay extra to reach their destinations.
The counter-based Metro Prabhati service is failing to meet passenger demand. The buses operate between the city’s northern areas and Patenga Sea Beach. Although they are supposed to leave every five minutes, commuters often wait 20–30 minutes for a bus.
During peak hours, standing passengers reportedly outnumber those who get seats. Many are forced to travel standing despite paying comparatively high fares.
Despite having 72 buses, BRTC has a limited presence on regular city routes. Ten operate as school buses, while 18 serve students and teachers of different universities. Others run on long-distance routes, including Chittagong-Rangamati, Chittagong-Khagrachhari, Chittagong-Sylhet and Chittagong-Dhaka.
BRTC Bus Depot and Training Centre Manager (Operations) Kamruzzaman said the buses under the Chittagong unit operate on various routes, including 10 school buses.
Chittagong Metropolitan Bus Owners’ Association President Belayet Hossain Belal said the shortage is most acute during office hours. He said 65–70% of permitted buses are engaged in transporting industrial workers during peak periods, leaving ordinary commuters with fewer options. He also attributed the lack of new buses to rising vehicle prices and declining returns.
Chittagong Metropolitan Police Assistant Commissioner (Public Relations) Aminur Rashid said the traffic division was working to maintain discipline. Legal action and fines were being imposed against traffic violators, while AI-based cameras were being installed to strengthen traffic monitoring.

item.title: Applications pour in for fertilizer dealership in Ctg
item.description:
Applications have poured in for the recruitment of fertilizer dealers in Chittagong, with 1,010 applications submitted so far against 384 posts in 16 upazilas of the district and the city.
The Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE) issued the recruitment notice on August 21 to appoint dealers to sell fertilizer to farmers. Although September 10 is the final date for applications, 1,010 applications had been submitted, according to DAE.
The recruitment will cover 29 dealer positions across 15 unions and two municipalities in Mirsarai, 18 in Sitakunda, 11 in north Fatikchhari, 25 in Fatikchhari municipality and 11 unions, 33 in Hathazari, one in Hathazari areas under City Corporation Ward-1, 30 in Raozan, 32 in Rangunia, 24 in Boalkhali, 34 in Patiya, 10 in Karnaphuli, 24 in Anwara, 15 in Chandanaish, four in Lohagara, 27 in Satkania, 28 in Banshkhali and 37 in Sandwip.
In addition, one fertilizer dealer each will be appointed in Panchlaish and Patenga areas of Chittagong City Corporation.
Applicants are required to submit national identity cards and citizenship certificates, three recent passport-size photographs, trade licences, documents detailing ownership or rental agreement for the proposed shop and warehouse, and recent bank solvency certificates.
They must also submit a signed list of family members, certified by a local public representative, including parents, sons, unmarried daughters and dependent siblings, as well as a certificate confirming submission of the latest income tax return.
A visit to the DAE office found applicants submitting their forms directly at the office conference room. Officials assigned to the process were checking and receiving the applications.
Although long queues of applicants were seen during the initial days of the process, the rush has eased in recent days. Officials said 1,010 applications had been received by Thursday afternoon.
DAE Deputy Director Apru Marma said that applications were being accepted for the appointment of fertilizer dealers. “The initial deadline for submitting applications was August 31. Later, the deadline was extended. The current deadline is September 10,” he said.

item.title: Nahid: Country is somewhat stable, but needs strong foundation
item.description:
National Citizen Party (NCP) convener and opposition chief whip Nahid Islam has said the situation in the country remains somewhat stable, but a strong foundation must be established to ensure communal harmony, human dignity and stronger democratic institutions.
“We are still continuing that movement,” he said.
Nahid made the remarks at a press briefing after a view-exchange meeting with members of the Sanatan community at Dhakeshwari Temple in the capital on Friday, on the occasion of Janmashtami. NCP Joint Member Secretary and MP Nusrat Tabassum and other central leaders were present.
Nahid said the country had previously witnessed various forms of torture and oppression against minorities and ethnic communities, while the state or government remained silent and failed to take action.
“Sometimes, it indirectly supported them. Due to this, a culture of impunity was created,” he said.
“From that place, after the July uprising, we have repeatedly said that the judiciary must be strengthened. Communal harmony and human dignity must be ensured,” he added.
Nahid said the implementation of the July Charter and the verdict of the referendum would help establish the judiciary on a strong foundation.
“We think that if the July Charter and the referendum verdict are implemented, the country's judiciary will stand on a strong foundation. Through this, there will be a place for people of all communities in the country to get justice,” he said.
“All political forces, including the government and the opposition, must keep this in mind. The culture of impunity must be changed. Political and democratic institutions must be strengthened,” he added.
He said the country had a spiritual bond with people of all religions, including the Hindu community.
“Their festivals are thousands of years old, and the interaction of people of many cultures and religions in this delta has developed through interactive communication. Such a bond must be maintained,” Nahid said.
He called on followers of Sanatan Dharma to pray for the people of Bangladesh and the NCP.

Health minister vows to make all government hospitals free of brokers
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Friday vowed to make all government hospitals in the country free of brokers.
He made the remarks while briefing journalists after inspecting Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College Hospital, the 250-bed District Hospital and Shaheed Shamsuddin Ahmad Hospital in Sylhet.
Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir was present at the briefing.
The health minister also directed the authorities concerned to resolve all drainage and cleanliness problems at hospitals in Sylhet within 7 days.
He said a syndicate lures patients to private clinics with false promises.
Sakhawat said all law enforcement agencies, including the Directorate General of Forces Intelligence (DGFI) and Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), are working together to identify and curb such broker syndicates.
“Their activities have already been reduced,” he said.
Regarding the ongoing drive against illegal clinics and fake doctors, he said mobile courts are being conducted regularly in the districts through deputy commissioners and civil surgeons, with illegal establishments being fined and sealed off.
The minister said clinics providing medical services, including surgeries, through unauthorized doctors and technicians holding fake certificates are also being sealed off.
He said he is personally collecting lists of such establishments and supervising the drives against them.
Asked about doctors’ attendance at hospitals, Sakhawat said he has visited more than 25 hospitals over the past month and found doctors fully present.
He added that patients have also reported improvements in doctors’ behavior and the quality of food served at hospitals.
On the measles outbreak, the minister said the number of unvaccinated children in the country has increased as regular measles vaccination campaigns were not held for a long time after December 2020, resulting in the spread of the disease.
He said some children who became eligible for vaccination after the campaign, as well as those who missed vaccination on time due to a lack of awareness, remained unvaccinated, allowing measles to spread among them.
Sakhawat said vaccination activities are continuing with adequate vaccines brought in with support from the World Bank and UNICEF.

item.title: Martinelli joins Al-Hilal from Arsenal for reported £60 million
item.description:
Arsenal forward Gabriel Martinelli has joined Saudi side Al-Hilal, the Premier League champions announced Thursday.
No fee was disclosed but British media reports said the deal was worth a guaranteed £60 million ($81 million).
That would make 25-year-old Brazil international Martinelli the most expensive player to leave the London club, following Alex Oxlade Chamberlain's £35 million exit to Liverpool in 2017.
Martinelli has signed a four-year deal with Al-Hilal, who are currently joint-top of the Saudi Pro League with Cristiano Ronaldo's Al-Nassr.
"Gabriel Martinelli has joined Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal on a permanent transfer," said a statement on Arsenal's website.
"Proud to be blue, proud to be Al-Hilal," said Martinelli during an unveiling video on his new club's social media channels.
He will join Ollie Watkins at Al-Hilal after the England striker left Aston Villa in a deal worth an estimated £51 million.
Martinelli's departure comes after Arsenal sold fellow left-sided forward Leandro Trossard to Besiktas.
Christos Tzolis has joined from Club Brugge but there are concerns the exits of Martinelli and Trossard could leave Arsenal short of personnel in that part of the pitch.
Martinelli made 53 appearances in all competitions last season, scoring 11 goals, as the Gunners won the top-flight title for the first time since 2004.
His nearly 300 games for Arsenal, including 62 goals, also saw him involved in their 2020 FA Cup and 2023 Community Shield successes.
But he was left out of Arsenal's first two matchday squads of the season, with manager Mikel Arteta making it clear Martinelli would struggle for game time were he to remain at the Emirates Stadium.
Former Arsenal striker Ian Wright criticised the club's decision to omit Martinelli from the squad for the opening game against Coventry.
"The way Martinelli is being treated at the moment, it really makes me feel uncomfortable," Wright told Sky Sports.
"I know they might want him out, and a lot of people might say, 'yeah, it's time for him to move him on'. But there's ways of doing that and it should suit him as well, how he wants to leave."

item.description:
SOCCER-SPAIN-BET-RMA/

Real Madrid’s perfect start to the LaLiga season ended on Friday when Real Betis beat them 1-0, with substitute Troy Parrott scoring nine minutes from time and goalkeeper Alvaro Valles saving a stoppage-time penalty from Kylian Mbappe.

The clash began at a high tempo but the pace dropped after the interval in the heat in Seville. Parrott, introduced in the 68th minute, broke the deadlock in the 81st when he reacted quickly after Real goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois parried a header into his path.

Mbappe struck the crossbar four minutes later before substitute Carlos Espi met a cross from Vinicius Junior with a spectacular bicycle kick, only for the equaliser to be ruled out for offside following a VAR review.

Nelson Deossa then nearly sealed the victory for hosts Betis with a long-range effort after spotting Courtois off his line, but the goalkeeper recovered to make the save.

Madrid got one final opportunity when Natan brought down Vinicius inside the area deep into stoppage time, but Valles saved Mbappe's spot kick to preserve Betis's lead and secure the three points.

item.title: An appetite for aloo bhorta, shorshe salmon and wrestling
item.description:
How can you not love a book that begins with aloo bhorta, that spicy mashed potato concoction that sets the tone of the novel. It's ostensibly a simple dish, but filled with all sorts of ingredients and nuances that sets it aside from the commonplace -- I'm talking about both the bhorta and the book here!

Set in the US, the novel Appetite revolves around a young woman, perched somewhat precariously on the threshold of her career. Precariously, because she is breaking away from the South Asian mould of studying to be a doctor or engineer or any such "respectable" profession, and ventures into the world of gastronomy. This is Zarina, the central character of the book, who we find in the kitchen of the restaurant Zero's where she may still be at a sous chef level, but she certainly knows her thyme from her tarragon. And she never loses a chance to throw in a bit of her Bangladeshi culinary skills, like when she impresses chef Anna Callahan by jazzing up a rather bland fish dish and conjuring up shorshe salmon with a dash of mustard. Zarina places Chef Callahan on a pedestal and praise from her means the world.

And here comes the parallel part of Zarina's life and, indeed, of the novel. Just as she is passionate about cooking and views Anna with awe, there is a whole other world that consumes her attention. This is Wrestle Thunder Ground, better known to fans as WTG. It's kinda like WWE (formerly WWF), but for women wrestlers. And Zarina's obsession is with the wrestler Sierra Myst, flamboyant and arrogant as these wrestlers are wont to be. (Perhaps a cross between Hulk Hogan and Stone Cold Steve Austin of the classic WWF era!)

In creating this fictitious wrestling federation WTG, the young author P Paramita actually reveals an interesting social change. Back in the days of the WWF manosphere, women wrestlers were used as gimmicks to attract crowds. Here they are an established part of professional wrestling, on par with their male counterparts.

Also interesting is how she readily accepts that these wrestling matches are scripted and expresses her appreciation by drawing up an analogy between this sport and cooking:

"Knowing someone was crafting these stories for me made me fall even deeper in love. Creating a successful wrestling match is very much like creating the perfect dish. Finding the right rivalry, the perfect storyline, getting audience attention by trial and error of mixing up different wrestlers in the ring reminds me of picking out the right ingredients, getting the perfect flavor combination, and tasting the marriage of a mixture of perfectly calibrated flavors."

Replete with Twitter (she stubbornly refuses calling it X) interactions of the Sierra Myst fandom, the book builds up the craze of the near frenzied fans and even the reader gets caught up in the wave of adulation and excitement when Zarina actually gets to interact with her idol Sierra, first on social media and then in real life!

Zarina is steadily sucked more and more into the heady world of fandom. While she is still a dedicated chef, we see how being a Sierra Myst follower places demands on her time and energy. She is charmed by Sierra, grateful to have her attention and is quite blind to the possibility that she, as an "influencer" is being used as a tool to further the star's stardom.

P Paramita is adept at drawing up parallels. We see the inevitable jealousies in Zero's kitchen as well as among the Sierra Myst followers. There is also a contrast between the two women she admires so much -- Chef Anna Callahan is kind and level-headed, an appreciative mentor. Sierra Myst is wild, outrageous, the all-out star who can be charming to the hilt.

There is something endearing about Zarina. She may be rebelling, not heeding her parents' dreams of "greater things" for her, but nostalgia does kick in from time to time. While squeezing lime over her food and mixing her rice and dal, she transported back home when she was just a child and her mother would cajole her into eating by making little balls of rice -- "This is a parrot's egg. This is a magpie's egg." Ironically, phone calls with her mother predictably end up with her mother saying, "How much longer are you going to waste your time playing chef?"

Zarina has been rooted in Bangladesh, not in any jingoistic or overt manner, but in small things. Asserting her Bangladeshi taste in food, rejecting Sierra's blanket perceptions of her being Indian, seeking out a sweet shop in Jackson Heights...

Zarina goes through a bit of introspection. It dawns on her that at home her worth is determined by whether she has a medical degree or not. Online her worth is how much attention she can muster from Sierra Myst. She feels invisible, easily replaceable. But becoming visible seems like a faraway dream.

She does have a dream of opening a Bengali fusion restaurant, but a futile dream at the moment as it means an investment she cannot afford. There is a glimmer of hope when chef Anna shows interest. Anna is the rock she needs, telling her, "I believe in you."

Her pride in being a Bengali is also revealed when she is explaining to a friend, "In Bangla we don't have gendered pronouns. It feels liberating." Ah, that's a great point to remember. We don't have the need to go onto all that pronoun rigmarole. Thanks, P Paramita, we knew that before, but now we are more conscious of it!

Back to the WTG world and Zarina herself is being thrust into a sort of parallel stardom as being perhaps the No.1 Sierra fan whom Sierra acknowledges and promotes. That comes with the barbs and acidic comments of the rival fans too, who call her clingy and desperate.
The story takes us through Zarina's choppy journey alternating between the glamorous tinsel world of WTG and the wholesome but challenging culinary world.

When the reader sees Zarina's relationship with Sierra Myst gradually disintegrating, there is trepidation of hurtful disillusionment and humiliation. True, that is all there, but there is also a sense of pride and dignity where Zarina stands tall and refuses to be used by Myst. What is a skillful twist by the writer P Paramita, is that she doesn't make Sierra into the stereotypical bad woman. She makes her human, a women with her fair share of heartbreaks and it is Zarina who chooses to firmly end the relationship.

The biggest adrenaline rush is not the fighting in the ring or the wrestling championship. It is Zarina fighting against all odds, lining up with true friends (yes, Anna is one of them -- we were so anxious of a fall out in that friendship!) and finally opening up a restaurant of her own. ROOT. What an appropriate name. Throughout the novel Zarina has been rooted in Bangladesh, not in any jingoistic or overt manner, but in small things. Asserting her Bangladeshi taste in food, rejecting Sierra's blanket perceptions of her being Indian, seeking out a sweet shop in Jackson Heights and so many other small details.

Somewhere at the outset of the book Zarina had said, "The secret of a good aloo bhorta is the marriage of five ingredients: potatoes, mustard oil, ghee, chillis and red onions." That seems to be the secret of P Paramita's book Appetite. A dash of desperation, a pinch of passion and dollop of dedication... and voila! A story that whets our appetite for her next book!

item.title: Cambodia scam centre: Man freed after being held captive for 17 days
item.description:
Mohammad Shafiqul Islam went to Cambodia through a manpower agent in the hope of getting a computer data-entry job. But after arriving there, his passport and mobile phone were taken away. He was held captive and tortured for refusing to engage in online scams. The 30-year-old man claimed he was released after paying $3,200.

According to Shafiqul, he returned home after a harrowing 22-day experience in Cambodia. During this time, he was held captive for 17 days at an alleged ‘scam centre’. He said he was regularly beaten and subjected to electric shocks, while being given insufficient food. He was also allegedly being put up for sale.

Shafiqul lives with his wife, a son and a daughter in Mirpur, Dhaka. He had been running a fire-safety equipment business for around eight years. After becoming acquainted on Facebook with a man named Mohammad Masud Mia, he was offered a job abroad. At one point, he was sent to Cambodia on the promise of a data-entry job on a computer.

This correspondent verified some of Shafiqul’s passport, travel documents and financial transaction information. However, his account of being held captive, tortured and allegedly put up for sale in Cambodia could not be independently verified.

Tk 450,000 agreement

Shafiqul said that before going to Cambodia, he learned basic computer skills. On 1 September last year, he signed an agreement with Masud for Tk 450,000 on a Tk 200 stamp paper. He also completed three days of training by the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) at the Probashi Kalyan Bhaban in Dhaka and received a clearance certificate, which is a smart card. His flight was initially scheduled for 16 October, but it was later rescheduled for 26 October.

After arriving at the airport in Dhaka, immigration police stopped Shafiqul. He was told to have his smart card verified at the Probashi Desk. Shafiqul said, “There was a woman at the Probashi Desk. She was scanning and verifying everyone’s cards. After I handed over my passport, she saw my name and let me go without verification. When I went back to immigration, the police allowed me to proceed.”

However, after arriving in Cambodia, Shafiqul was stopped by the country’s immigration authorities. Police seized and kept his passport. He then contacted a man named Mostafa Mukul, an associate of Masud who was staying in Cambodia, by phone from Phnom Penh airport. After a while, the police officer concerned checked the messages on Shafiqul’s phone. Shafiqul claimed that his employment visa was later changed to a tourist visa. He was then allowed to leave the airport.

Calling and chatting scams

Arif, an associate of Mukul, was waiting outside Phnom Penh airport. Shafiqul reached a residential building 40 minutes later in an auto-rickshaw with him. In the meantime, Arif took $800 from him. By the time they arrived, it was night. He was given some food and told that there would be an interview shortly.

Suddenly, at around 1:00 am, another person was put into the car with Shafiqul. At around 8:00 am on 27 October, they arrived at a complex near the Thailand border. Inside the compound, which was surrounded by boundary walls, there were three six-storey buildings. The two were accommodated on the third floor of one building. Their workplace was on the fifth floor of the same building.

According to Shafiqul, the entire compound was much like a prison. There was no way to leave. Security guards were stationed all around. His mobile phone and passport were taken away. He was made to sign a document written in Chinese, which was then kept by them. He was subsequently given two scripts, one in Hindi and another in English, and told to memorise them. They spent a day this way. Work began on 28 October. He was assigned to the ‘calling room’.

Shafiqul said it was basically a ‘scam centre’, which was owned by the Chinese, and operated by the Pakistanis. There were two departments here: calling and chatting.

In the calling department, there were four stages. The first-line workers called 500 numbers a day from a list to verify names and addresses. They mainly targeted Indians. After collecting the initial information, the case was passed to the second line. They called to verify Aadhaar cards (Indian citizens’ identity cards).

After obtaining this information, the third line was the police station. They made video calls pretending to be police officers, and the entire room was decorated to resemble a police station. One or two people were handcuffed and placed in the background, pretending to be accused persons. Threats were made.

The fourth stage involved a room designed like a bank. They called the same customer, demanded a fine in the name of the police, collected some more information and asked for the PIN number.

Meanwhile, the bank account was hacked and all the money was stolen. This was how the scam operated in four stages.

The work in the chatting room is different. They mainly operate profiles created in women's names on various social media platforms (Facebook, Instagram and dating apps). This group works from 11:00 pm until 11:00 am the following day. They target US citizens and lure them into romantic relationships.

While chatting, they eventually talk over audio calls. Although men speak on the calls, software makes the voice heard on the other end sound like a woman's voice. This helps create trust. They gradually collect information this way and then use hacking to steal money from the US citizens.

Released after 22 days

Shafiqul said that on 28 October, he and another man named Ishtiaq Rabbi joined the second stage of work in the calling room. Most of the people working at the centre were Pakistani.

There were also some Bangladeshis and Indians. Two days later, when they refused to work, the two were handcuffed and detained. That night, there was an interview, and Rabbi was sold. Shafiqul was then subjected to torture.

Shafiqul said he was subjected to electric shocks and beatings. They repeatedly tried to sell him but failed. Suddenly, on 16 November, they released him and put him in a vehicle.

The vehicle took him to Siem Reap and dropped him off at an isolated location. His passport and mobile phone were returned. After he requested help, the driver took him to a bus station and bought him a ticket to Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia.

Shafiqul spoke to his family by phone. He learned that his younger brother had sought help from the Bangladeshi community in Cambodia. They had paid $3,200 and arranged for his release from the scam centre.

After reaching Phnom Penh, he stayed at the home of a community representative. After staying there for two days, a ticket was arranged from Bangladesh and he returned home on 18 November empty-handed.

After returning home, Shafiqul spoke to the broker, Masud. Masud claimed that he did not know about the attempt to sell him. He also promised to provide compensation. Since then, Masud has been untraceable. His office is also closed. Shafiqul is preparing to file a case.

Shafiqul said he had endured torture and abuse. Since he has received neither compensation nor justice, he now seeks the government's assistance.

The power of thinking and questioning
item.description:
More than three centuries ago, French philosopher René Descartes coined the famous phrase Cogito, ergo sum (I think, therefore I am) to define the essence of human existence.
His statement suggests that our ability to think is what makes us conscious, aware, and uniquely human. Because of the ability to think, human beings are often regarded as the most intelligent creatures on Earth.
Yet an important question remains: How many of us truly think, and how many think effectively?
In today's fast-paced world, there is a fine line between thinking and overthinking. Unfortunately, whenever someone pauses to analyze an issue deeply, question assumptions, or explore different possibilities, they are often labeled an “overthinker.”
As a result, many people become hesitant to ask questions or challenge conventional ideas.
However, progress has never come from unquestioned acceptance. Every invention, discovery, and social transformation began when someone dared to think differently and ask a simple but powerful question: “Why?”
Innovation is not merely about creating new technology; it is about developing new ways of understanding and solving problems. In a world facing increasingly complex challenges, the ability to think critically and question intelligently is a necessity.
If we look around Bangladesh, we will find no shortage of crises.
Every monsoon, floods affect millions of people, disrupting education, livelihoods, and communication.
In our cities, traffic congestion consumes valuable hours that could otherwise be spent on productive activities.
Plastic waste blocks drainage systems, contributing to urban flooding, while environmental pollution continues to threaten public health.
These problems are often discussed, criticized, and debated. Yet meaningful solutions emerge only when people move beyond complaints and begin asking the right questions.
Take the issue of urban flooding. Instead of merely blaming heavy rainfall, an innovative mind asks: Why do roads remain submerged long after the rain stops? Are drainage systems inadequate? Is unmanaged waste preventing water from flowing properly?
Such questions encourage us to investigate root causes rather than visible symptoms. Once the causes are identified, practical solutions become easier to design, whether through improved waste management, better urban planning, or community awareness campaigns.
Similarly, traffic congestion is not simply a transportation problem; it is also a thinking problem.
Every day, thousands of people lose valuable time on the roads. But what if students, engineers, and policy-makers worked together to rethink public transportation? What if technology could be used to monitor traffic flow more efficiently? What if flexible working hours reduced rush-hour pressure?
Progress begins when people challenge the assumption that existing conditions are unavoidable.
The same principle applies to education. Many students in remote areas still face barriers to quality learning. Rather than accepting this reality, innovators ask how digital technologies, community-based learning initiatives, or low-cost educational resources can bridge the gap.
Every educational advancement begins with someone identifying a problem and refusing to believe that it cannot be solved.
Innovation is not limited to laboratories, scientists, or large corporations. It begins with observation. It grows through curiosity. It develops through questioning.
A student who wonders how to reduce food waste in the cafeteria, save electricity in classrooms, or improve the campus environment is already thinking like an innovator.
The goal is not simply to find answers but to cultivate the habit of asking meaningful questions.
As Bangladesh moves toward a future shaped by rapid technological advancement and global challenges, the country will need more than skilled workers. It will need critical thinkers, problem-solvers, and innovators.
The next breakthrough idea may not come from a famous inventor or a multinational company. It may come from a student who dares to ask a question that others overlook.
Thinking is not a luxury but a responsibility. Questioning is not a sign of weakness but the beginning of wisdom. Every crisis carries within it an opportunity for innovation.
The moment we stop accepting problems as permanent and start questioning them, we take the first step toward meaningful change.
After all, every great solution begins with a simple question: “What if there is a better way?”
Md Inzamul Haque is a lecturer at the Department of English, Southeast University.

Travel has lost some of its old appeal in the global age, aided by instantaneous internet communication and the relative ease of travelling long distances.
In the old days, travel had a special meaning, particularly when the destination was a faraway country and the journey itself involved flying across continents.
Globalization, we are told, has killed distance. These days, hardly any place seems truly far away. Internet-mediated communication has also, in a sense, diminished culture shock.
Whether viscerally, in person, or virtually, we have already seen so much of the world. We can watch its streets, its people, its food, its politics and its landscapes on our screens.
Yet travelogue is not dead yet.
It is the unexpected encounters and experiences for which we are rarely prepared that make travelling worthwhile.
Zadar: Where nature plays music
In Zadar, an ancient Croatian city on the Adriatic coast, we encountered something that could hardly be experienced through a computer screen: The Sea Organ.
Built into the waterfront, it produces music through the movement of the waves. The sea itself becomes the musician.
As the waves enter the organ's pipes, they generate sounds that rise and fall unpredictably. Nearby, the Sun Salutation -- another remarkable installation -- responds to sunlight with a different kind of spectacle.
Between the sea, the sunset and the installations, Zadar offers something close to a symphony of nature and human creativity.
The waves of the Adriatic not only catch the eye; they soothe the ear.
That is perhaps what travel does best. It brings together things that we may know intellectually but have never actually experienced.
Education, sport, and Croatia
We attended a workshop at the University of Zadar, an institution that goes back to 1396, one of the oldest universities in East Europe.
Later, we met members of the city council. Their offices were decorated with large posters of famous Croatian football stars. It was football season, and the national team was very much on people's minds.
I asked a simple question: How does a country of fewer than four million people repeatedly produce athletes capable of competing at the highest level of international sport?
Football, of course, is only part of the story. Croatia has also produced world-class athletes in tennis, skiing, rowing, water polo, handball, athletics, and other sports. The country's sporting achievements are remarkable relative to its small population.
Sport is taken seriously as part of children's education and community life. Croatia has a national sports program that explicitly links sport with the educational system and sets responsibilities for national and local authorities, while its education system includes physical education and opportunities for students to pursue sport more intensively.
The idea that education, sport, music, and community life could be treated as complementary components of a child's development struck me.
Migrants far from home
Croatia also has experienced a significant increase in foreign workers, including workers from Nepal who are quite visible. Bangladeshis were present too though in much smaller numbers.
I had conversations with Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia during their work breaks. They seemed pleasantly surprised that people they described as bhadralok -- people from the educated and relatively privileged sections of society -- would simply stop and talk to them on the sidewalk.
Many described precarious lives: Insecure employment, uncertain immigration status, and limited social support.
One worker told me something that stayed with me. When ministers and senior officials from Dhaka visited Malaysia, he said, they often met Bengali businesspeople, community leaders, and embassy officials but had little time to meet the ordinary workers whose remittances make such an important contribution to Bangladesh's economy.
I wondered: Why should it be so difficult to talk to the people who do some of the hardest work and whose earnings contribute so substantially to the country's foreign-exchange reserves?
Perhaps governments everywhere need to remember that migrants are not merely sources of remittances. They are citizens, workers, and human beings whose experiences provide an important measure of how a country values its people.
Australia: Democracy and the welfare state
In Australia, I spent some quiet time at the Museum of Australian Democracy at Old Parliament House in Canberra.
The building was Australia's federal Parliament from 1927 until 1988, when Parliament moved to the new Parliament House on Capital Hill. In 2009, the old building became the home of the Museum of Australian Democracy.
Walking through the museum was an encounter with Australia's political memory. I came across displays devoted to former prime ministers, including references to their education and careers.
Among them was Robert -- Bob -- Hawke, whom I had briefly encountered in Adelaide in 2015. Hawke, then in a wheelchair, appeared at a conference I was attending. He came to our session, and I had the opportunity to shake his hand and exchange a few words with him.
When I met him, I reminded him that I had been a graduate student in the United States when he became prime minister and had read about his life in The New York Times. That was how I knew about his Rhodes Scholarship.
He seemed pleased that I remembered it. But I had the impression that, for Hawke, being a Rhodes Scholar was not what defined his life.
His real accomplishments, in his own eyes, were his leadership of the trade union movement and his service as prime minister.
That distinction is worth remembering. Education can open doors, but what a person does with that education is ultimately more important than the credential itself.
Australia also offers an interesting example of the welfare state in everyday life.
Habibul Haque Khondker is a sociologist and columnist.

item.title: Ninth national pay scale: The real test
item.description:
Public employees deserve fair wages. But a government pay scale is never only about government employees.
When millions of households are already struggling with high prices, weak purchasing power, and economic uncertainty, a large public-sector wage increase inevitably becomes a question of wider economic justice.
That is why the approval of the ninth national pay scale deserves to be examined not simply as a salary revision, but as a major macro-economic policy decision.
The new pay structure raises basic salaries by up to 142%, with the minimum basic salary rising to Tk20,000 and the maximum to Tk1,56,000. Full implementation is expected to require an additional Tk106,000 crore annually.
The question is not whether government employees deserve better pay. They do. The harder question is: How can Bangladesh implement such a large wage adjustment without making life even more expensive for everyone else?
Bangladesh is entering this reform with little room for complacency. Headline inflation stood at 8.32% in July 2026, while non-food inflation remained higher at 9.28%. The average inflation rate for FY2025–26 was 8.68%.
For a salaried household, these numbers are not abstract economic indicators. They mean that the same income buys less food, transport, education, healthcare, and other necessities than it did before.
And the burden is not evenly distributed.
According to the latest Labour Force Survey 2024, around 84% of employed people -- approximately 5.80 crore workers -- are engaged in informal employment.
These workers do not receive a government pay revision every few years. Many have no automatic cost-of-living adjustment, no guaranteed annual increment, and limited protection against sudden price increases.
This creates the central distributional dilemma of pay scale: A wage increase for millions of public employees can be justified, but who protects the millions who have no employer capable of passing higher costs on to someone else?
Of course, the pay scale alone will not cause Bangladesh’s inflation. That would be economically simplistic. Inflation has multiple drivers -- exchange rates, food supply, import costs, energy prices, market concentration, fiscal and monetary conditions, and global commodity shocks.
But a major wage-driven increase in aggregate demand can add pressure when supply-side constraints are already severe.
The transmission mechanism is straightforward:
Government wages rise → consumption rises → prices respond → private employees demand higher wages → business costs increase → investment and competitiveness suffer → inflationary pressure persists.
This concern is not simply theoretical. Business leaders have already warned that higher public-sector wages could increase pressure on the private sector, particularly labour-intensive industries already struggling with energy shortages, high borrowing costs, and an unstable business environment.
If private employers respond by raising wages, they may also face higher production costs. If they cannot absorb those costs, prices may rise. If they cannot raise prices because of weak demand or international competition, investment and employment may suffer.
This is where Bangladesh needs to look beyond the government payroll.
The latest external economic outlook is hardly reassuring. The World Bank has projected Bangladesh’s FY2025–26 growth at only 3.9%, citing elevated inflation, weak investment, financial-sector vulnerabilities, and the effects of the Middle East conflict.
It has also warned that poverty has already increased and that further shocks could push more people below the poverty line.
Recent shocks have pushed up international prices of energy and agricultural inputs, with crude oil, LNG, and nitrogen fertilizer prices all experiencing significant increases.
For Bangladesh, this matters enormously. Higher energy and fertilizer costs eventually reach farmers, transport operators, manufacturers, and consumers.
The agricultural economy is particularly vulnerable. According to FAO, around 10 lakh agricultural households -- nearly 50 lakh people -- are projected to need emergency agricultural assistance during June-November 2026.
These numbers should force a broader question: While the state increases the purchasing power of public employees, what is the state’s plan for protecting the purchasing power of everyone else?
At present, Bangladesh’s social safety-net system is not designed to function as a universal shield against inflation. Informal workers, low-income households, small producers, and many private-sector employees remain highly exposed to economic shocks.
A pay scale without a parallel protection strategy risks creating a two-speed economy: One group receives an institutionalized income adjustment, while another absorbs the consequences through higher prices and weaker real wages.
That would be economically inefficient and socially unfair.
What should be done?
First, establish a pay scale-inflation monitoring framework. The government should monitor the impact of the new pay structure on inflation, consumption, private-sector wages, employment, and fiscal sustainability.
If inflationary pressures intensify significantly, subsequent phases of implementation should be reviewed rather than treated as automatic.
Second, protect workers beyond the public payroll. Temporary, targeted income support should be expanded for low-income informal workers and vulnerable households during periods of severe inflation. Social protection must become more responsive to economic shocks rather than functioning mainly as a collection of static programs.
Third, address the supply side. Wage reform cannot be separated from food security, energy reliability, fertilizer availability, import management, and market competition. If supply cannot respond to rising demand, wage increases will translate too easily into higher prices.
Fourth, finance the pay scale through structural reform rather than excessive fiscal pressure. Stronger domestic revenue mobilization, better tax compliance, expenditure rationalization, and improved public financial management are essential. Borrowing simply to finance recurrent wage and pension commitments would shift today's adjustment costs onto tomorrow's taxpayers.
Finally, Bangladesh must stop viewing wage policy, inflation policy, and social protection as separate policy silos. They are deeply interconnected.
A government employee struggling to pay rent and educate children deserves a decent salary.
But so does the garment worker whose wage does not automatically rise with inflation.
So does the rickshaw puller whose daily income is uncertain.
So does the small farmer face higher fertilizer and fuel costs.
So does the informal worker who has no pension, no paid leave, and no protection against economic shocks.
The real measure of the ninth national pay scale should therefore not be how much government employees receive on their pay slips. It should be whether Bangladesh can raise public-sector incomes without reducing the real incomes of millions outside the public sector.
The government has an opportunity to demonstrate that wage reform and economic stability do not have to be opposing goals. But that needs more than a new salary structure.
It requires a coherent macroeconomic strategy that manages inflation, protects vulnerable workers, strengthens supply chains, and ensures that fiscal reform is sustainable.
A pay rise for some should not become a price rise for everyone. That is the real test.
Amith Kumar Malaker is a human rights defender and public policy analyst based in Bangladesh.
